one_liner: Rust PDF toolkit (text, Markdown, images, editing) whose README claims 5x PyMuPDF; its own owner's later runs show it slower on real text-bearing PDFs.
what_it_does: A Rust PDF library for text, character, word, table, image and Markdown/HTML extraction, plus page rendering, form filling, merging and PDF creation. The Rust core ships as a crate, a CLI, an MCP server, a C ABI and bindings for 19 languages; the Python API (PdfDocument, page.text, page.markdown()) is shaped like PyMuPDF's but is not a drop-in replacement. Its stated motive is an MIT/Apache alternative to AGPL PyMuPDF.
how_it_is_fast: Its advantage is in fixed per-file cost: a nom-based lexer and lazy xref and object loading make document open cheap (owner's issue #1400 measured open 2.49x faster than PyMuPDF 1.28.2, winning on 39 of 54 files), and early-outs such as skipping pages without BT operators make text-free files nearly free (1 ms vs 15 ms on a veraPDF fixture). Glyph decoding runs at about PyMuPDF's whole-pipeline cost per character (0.93x), but char-to-word assembly takes 72-93% of extract_text time and makes text-heavy pages 2-5x slower than MuPDF or PDFium (issues #1389, #1400).
when_to_use: You need a permissively licensed (MIT or Apache-2.0) PDF text extractor where PyMuPDF's AGPL is unacceptable and some speed loss on text-heavy files is acceptable.
Bulk triage of many small or mostly text-free PDFs (conformance fixtures, scanned image-only files, metadata or page-count passes) where open time dominates; this is where the measured wins are.
You want one extraction core reachable from Rust, Python, Go, JS/WASM, C#, Java and others with the same output.
A pure-Rust build with no C toolchain in the default feature set (WASM, C# AOT, musl wheels).
when_not_to_use: Text extraction from ordinary text-bearing documents: the owner measured 0.47x PyMuPDF's speed on the mean over 200 real documents (median 853 KB) and 3.0x slower than PyMuPDF 1.28.2 on 54 documents on the v0.3.79 branch (issues #1387, #1400).
Long documents: page scaling measured O(n^1.33) vs PyMuPDF's O(n^0.80), about 2.6x slower at 512 pages; a 10,000-page veraPDF file exceeded 30 s where PyMuPDF took 3.96 s (#1387, #1389).
Rendering: 72 dpi RGBA rendering measured 3.4x slower than PyMuPDF (#1400, 2026-09-24).
Memory-constrained hosts: peak RSS about 2.1-2.2x PyMuPDF (32-36 MB vs 15-16 MB mean, #1387).

Multithreaded extraction of one document: threads sharing a document scale to about 1.9x and 8 threads ran slower than 4 (#1589), and there is no parallel whole-document extraction from Python (#2284).

integration.form: crate (also Python wheels via PyO3, a C ABI cdylib, CLI and WASM package)
integration.dependencies: Pure-Rust stack by default (qcms ICC, RustCrypto with legacy-crypto); optional C deps behind features: lcms2 (icc-lcms2), aws-lc-rs (fips), tract-onnx/pdfium-render (ml, ocr)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.88 (MSRV in Cargo.toml); Python >=3.9 on PyPI (the README still says 3.8)
integration.platforms: Wheels for Linux x86-64 and aarch64 (manylinux_2_28 and musllinux_1_2), macOS x86-64 and arm64, Windows x64 and arm64; WASM
integration.thread_safety: Not documented in what was read; issue #1589 reports poor scaling when threads share one document, and a Rust ParallelExtractor exists (repeats the document-wide artifact pass per worker, #2284).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — similar page-oriented Python API to PyMuPDF and pypdfium2, but different names and output; text, words and Markdown differ in layout from MuPDF's

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the headline: the README table's corpus is 2,907 veraPDF fixtures out of 3,830 files, with a median file of 3.8 KB and 76.2% of files yielding zero characters from either library; the owner's own same-work interleaved runs give 2.83x faster on veraPDF but 0.47x on real documents, and 0.31x vs PyMuPDF and 0.23x vs pypdfium2 on a 25-document mix (issues #1387, #1400, #1352). Issue #2275 (2026-10-07) states the 5x claim has not been verified on real files. The README still carries 0.8 ms and '5x faster'.

The table's runner is not published: scripts/bench_pymupdf.py times only the PyMuPDF side, bench/ has no Python runner (#2543), and the older scripts/benchmark_all_libraries.py times pdf_oxide's to_markdown_all against PyMuPDF's get_text with the output-file write inside the timer, so the work differs by tool.

'100% pass rate' rounds 7 failing files out (pdf.js suite 99.2%), and scripts/bench_compare.py counts pymupdf errors, 'oxide has more text' and any output whose character set is a superset of PyMuPDF's as clean, so the 99.5% parity figure is lenient.

Before 0.3.78 (2026-09-09) self-referential form XObjects could overflow the stack and five valid files aborted the host process, AES-256 encryption wrote files nothing could decrypt, and incremental updates dropped /Encrypt while appending plaintext objects; use 0.3.78 or later.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No PDF sibling is catalogued in string-and-text; the relevant listed baselines are MuPDF and PDFium (wave 10), which are faster on text-heavy documents per the owner's own runs. Pick PDFOxide only for licence (vs MuPDF's AGPL) or binding reach, or for open-dominated workloads of small files.
verified_claims_summary: The README reports a 0.8 ms mean per document vs 4.6 ms for PyMuPDF and 4.1 ms for pypdfium2 over 3,830 veraPDF, pdf.js and SafeDocs files, single thread, with no hardware, compiler or library versions and no published runner. The owner's later interleaved CPU-time runs (pdf_oxide 0.3.73 Python bindings, PyMuPDF 1.27.2.2, shared loaded machine) found 2.83x faster only on the veraPDF corpus and 0.47x on 200 real documents, and a 2026-09-24 rerun on the v0.3.79 branch found text 3.0x slower and open 2.49x faster than PyMuPDF 1.28.2.
status_note: Very active (0.3.78 on PyPI and crates.io 2026-09-08, 1.1k stars, 445 open issues, 1.24M crate downloads) and MIT/Apache-licensed, but the speed claim is contradicted by the maintainer's own issues #1387 and #1400 on text-bearing documents and holds only for open time and near-empty files; a retier below C (or a not-faster flag) is warranted.
